report.currency: USD (tables in millions unless stated; market reports natively in USD — no FX conversion required)
report.verdict: Pennsylvania's September 2026 print ($555.0m, +4.1% YoY) confirms a $7bn-a-year, online-led market: iGaming (+6.8%) and a hold-driven sports betting rebound (+50% taxable revenue on −6% handle) carried a −3.2% retail casino month. The numbers are strong but the rules are tightening — a bipartisan online consumer-protection push (HB 2879, PGCB Regulation 125-258), the post-Supreme Court skill-game shake-out and unlicensed sweepstakes/prediction-market competition define the 2027 agenda far more than tax risk does.
summary: **A $7bn market still compounding.** PGCB reported September 2026 combined gaming revenue of $555,036,870, +4.07% YoY versus $533.3m (−2.6% MoM from August's $569.7m). FY2025/26 (Jul-25 to Jun-26) closed at a record $7,006.0m (+9.6%), the first fiscal year above $7bn, with $3,098.2m returned in taxes and fees (44.2% of GGR, including $110m of slot-licence operation fees).

**Online is now the majority channel.** Online products — iGaming $249.3m, online sports taxable revenue $40.3m and fantasy $1.5m — generated $291.1m or 52.5% of September GGR; iGaming alone was 44.9% of the total (+1.2pp YoY). On a fiscal-year basis iGaming was 41.9% of GGR ($2,933.5m) and total online roughly 50%.

**iGaming: +6.8% YoY, but decelerating.** September iGaming GGR was $249.3m (+1.5% MoM): slots $197.4m (+9.0%), banking tables $49.7m (−0.6%), poker rake $2.3m (−1.8%). FY2025/26 growth was +18.4%; Q1 FY26/27 (Jul-Sep) is running at $744.0m. iSlots turnover was $5.12bn in the month at a 3.86% post-deduction hold.

**Sports betting is a hold story, not a volume story.** Handle fell 6.1% YoY to $798.7m, yet taxable revenue rose 50.5% to $44.7m because gross hold was 9.2% ($73.5m pre-promo) against a weak 3.5% taxable hold in September 2025. Promotional credits deducted were $28.8m (3.6% of handle; 39% of gross revenue). Online took 96.1% of handle and 90.2% of taxable revenue. FY2025/26: revenue $662.9m (+36.0%) on handle $8,448.1m (−3.1%); taxable hold 7.85% vs 5.59%.

**Retail casino is flat-to-soft.** Retail slots $196.2m (+2.4%; 24,523 units in service, +192 YoY; win/unit/day ≈ $267) and retail tables $60.2m (−18.1%) gave a combined $256.3m (−3.2% YoY, −8.6% MoM). FY2025/26 retail slots were +0.02% and tables −2.2%: the land-based base is ex-growth and iGaming is where incremental dollars land.

**Property league table is iGaming-weighted.** Hollywood Casino at Penn National Race Course reported $113.6m (20.5% of the state; +11.8%) on the back of $99.0m iGaming; Valley Forge $96.6m (17.4%; $69.8m iGaming + $15.8m sports); Rivers Philadelphia $55.7m; Parx $50.1m (−5.6%); Wind Creek Bethlehem $37.5m (−10.3%). Happy Valley Casino (Cat 4, opened April 2026) added $2.0m.

**iGaming is a three-licence market.** Penn National 39.7%, Valley Forge (FanDuel) 28.0% and Rivers Philadelphia 15.4% of September iGaming GGR — 83.1% combined; Harrah's (Caesars) 5.4%, Golden Nugget 2.9%, Parx 2.4%, Bally's 2.1%, Presque Isle 1.9%. Mount Airy ceased iGaming in September 2025; Mohegan (−64.6% YoY) and Wind Creek (−34.1%) are shrinking, Live! Philadelphia fell 52.8% over FY2025/26.

**Sports betting is a two-brand duopoly.** Valley Forge/FanDuel 37.9% of online taxable revenue (36.7% of online handle) and Hollywood Casino at the Meadows/DraftKings 30.7% (32.7%) — 68.6% together. Penn's York and Morgantown licences took 7.6% and 7.9%; Presque Isle's new online skin bought 5.3% of handle with promo credits equal to 86% of its gross revenue (taxable share 1.8%).

**Tax regime: GGR-based and among the heaviest in the US, but stable.** iSlots 54% (34% state + 13% CFA county grants + 5% LSA + 2% LSA); iTables/poker 16%; sports 36% (34% + 2%) of revenue net of promotional credits, plus the 0.25% federal excise on handle; retail slots ~55% statutory (34% state, Race Horse Development Fund ~12%, 5% EDTF, 4% local share) with a 50.6% effective rate in PGCB's September figures; retail tables 16% (17.4% effective); VGTs 52%; DFS 15%. September tax take $242.6m = 43.7% of GGR; iGaming $114.9m (46.1% effective); sports $16.1m.

**Promo deductibility materially lowers the effective burden.** Sportsbooks deducted $28.8m of credits in September (≈$10.4m of tax at 36%); the iGaming report implies $67.5m of deductions on slots (wagers $5,115.9m − payouts $4,851.1m − GGR $197.4m), i.e. ~25% of pre-deduction win, so the 54% headline bites on a materially smaller base. Q1 FY26/27 implied iSlots deductions: $213.3m.

**Licensing is casino-anchored.** 18 land-based casinos (6 Category 1 racetrack, 5 Category 2 stand-alone, 2 Category 3 resort, 5 Category 4 mini-casinos), 11 online sportsbooks, 17 retail books, 22 iGaming sites, 72 VGT truck stops (5 terminals each) and 7 DFS operators. Fees: interactive gaming certificate $10m for all three verticals (or $4m per vertical, also the Qualified Gaming Entity route for non-casino brands), sports wagering certificate $10m, both renewable at $250k every five years; platform-operator licence $1m/5 yrs ($100k renewal); $10m p.a. slot-licence operation fee for Cat 1/2; $4m bond per interactive certificate.

**Skill-game shake-out is the biggest structural event since Act 42.** The PA Supreme Court ruled in June 2026 that the estimated 70,000 'skill games' are slot machines under the Gaming Act and stayed enforcement 120 days; the legislature failed to act by 13 October and Pennsylvania State Police began seizures on 14 October, with Pace-O-Matic remotely disabling machines. This is a direct demand tailwind for licensed slots, VGTs and iGaming from Q4 2026 — until Harrisburg legalises and taxes the devices, which both parties and Gov. Shapiro say they want to do in 2027.

**Online consumer-protection push is bipartisan and specific.** HB 2879 (Pennsylvania Online Consumer Protection Act, introduced 21 Oct 2026 by Reps. Khan (D) and Flick (R) alongside a new Problem Gambling Caucus) would ban microbets and same-game parlays, VIP/host programmes and credit-card deposits; impose mandatory daily/monthly loss limits (lower for ages 21–25), a two-deposits-a-day cap, affordability checks above $5,000 in 180 days, a two-hour default daily session, biometric checks at login and for wagers above $500; restrict advertising; and levy 0.75% of online casino and sports revenue for DDAP problem-gambling programmes. It cannot pass before the session ends 30 November, but it is the template for 2027.

**PGCB is already moving by regulation.** Proposed Regulation #125-258 (Pennsylvania Bulletin, 11 Jul 2026) would require operators to offer daily/weekly/monthly deposit, spend, wager and time limits at account opening, hourly session pop-ups, monthly responsible-gambling messaging without promotions, direct-marketing opt-outs, account suspension up to a year, monthly self-limit/self-exclusion reporting and an advertising rule for majority-underage audiences. Comments closed 10 August; NCPG is lobbying for limits to be default-on; IRRC review is under way.

**The evidence base is state-commissioned.** The Joint State Government Commission's HR60 staff study (14 Jul 2026) ranks a player-data mandate first and recommends a uniform credit-card deposit ban for interactive accounts, mandatory self-limits, curbs on logged-off promotions and VIP programmes. The Penn State/DDAP 2025 Interactive Gaming Assessment (Jan 2026) found up to 30% of PA adults gambled online in 2025 (20% in 2024; ~11% in 2021-22), 2.5–6.4% may be problem gamblers, and >10% used unregulated sites.

**Unlicensed competition is on the 2027 docket.** HB 2801 (pre-filed late September for the session opening 5 Jan 2027) would ban online sweepstakes casinos with fines up to $500,000 and PGCB/Attorney General enforcement powers, inside a broader Gaming Act rewrite of fees, taxes and distributions. Prediction markets (Kalshi, Polymarket) operate in PA at 18+ outside PGCB; PGCB told the CFTC on 30 Apr 2026 that sports event contracts 'is sports wagering', while HB 2711 (22 Jul 2026) would instead license them under the Attorney General ($1m fee, 21+).

**Fiscal politics favour stability on rates.** The $50.8bn FY2026-27 budget (signed July 2026) contained no gaming tax changes; a record $3.1bn gaming take reduces near-term pressure for rate increases, and the live policy fight is over skill-game taxation (Shapiro has proposed taxing/regulating them in three of four budgets). The November 2026 gubernatorial election is the swing factor.

**Payments: card rails today, credit-card ban tomorrow.** Interactive accounts may be funded by credit card (retail slot play cannot be, under 58 Pa. Code), alongside ACH/online banking, debit, e-wallets and cage/prepaid options; PGCB publishes no payment-mix data (n/a). A credit-card ban is the single most probable payments rule change in 2027 (JSG recommendation + HB 2879).

**Read-through for B2Tech.** Market access is through a Pennsylvania casino skin or a Qualified Gaming Entity certificate ($4m per vertical) under a 54% slots tax — viable only with scale or as a B2B/platform supplier. iGaming (~$3bn, growing 7–18%) is the prize; sports betting is a FanDuel/DraftKings duopoly where entry is bought with promo (Presque Isle's 86% promo-to-gross). Underwrite 2027 for a credit-card ban, mandatory limits, promo/VIP curbs and a possible 0.75% RG levy rather than for a tax hike.

segments.name: Sports betting (online & retail)
segments.headline: Handle −6.1% YoY to $798.7m but taxable revenue +50.5% to $44.7m on a 9.2% gross hold; FanDuel and DraftKings hold 69% of online revenue while new entrants buy share with promo.
narrative: September is the first full NFL/college month and PGCB's data show the market has become structurally a hold story. Handle was $798.7m, down 6.1% on September 2025's $850.5m and the FY2025/26 handle of $8,448.1m was itself 3.1% below the prior year. Yet operator revenue before promotions was $73.5m (a 9.2% gross hold) and taxable revenue after $28.8m of deducted promotional credits was $44.7m, a 5.6% taxable hold against just 3.5% in September 2025 when favourites ran the table. Over FY2025/26 taxable hold rose to 7.85% from 5.59%, lifting revenue 36% on shrinking volume — the parlay-mix effect that is now the main growth engine, and the reason HB 2879's proposed ban on same-game parlays and microbets matters more to operators than any tax debate.

The promotional cycle is intense at season start. September's $28.8m of credits equalled 3.6% of handle and 39% of gross revenue, up from $11.1m (2.2% of handle) in August; across Q1 FY26/27 operators deducted $52.8m on $1,806.8m of handle (2.9%). Because Pennsylvania taxes sports revenue net of these credits at 36% (34% state plus 2% local share assessment), September's promotions saved operators roughly $10.4m of tax; the Commonwealth collected $16.1m. Hold and promo behaviour differ sharply by licensee: Valley Forge (FanDuel) ran a 9.2% gross hold with promo at 41% of gross; the Meadows (DraftKings) 8.2% and 40%; Harrah's (Caesars) 6.9% and 51%; Presque Isle, whose new online skin lifted its FY sports revenue more than tenfold, spent $4.43m of credits against $5.15m of gross revenue (86%), leaving only $0.72m taxable.

Online took 96.1% of handle ($767.5m) and 90.2% of taxable revenue ($40.3m); retail books across 17 locations handled $31.2m and won $4.4m. The online market is a duopoly: Valley Forge/FanDuel 36.7% of online handle and 37.9% of online taxable revenue, Hollywood Casino at the Meadows/DraftKings 32.7% and 30.7%. Penn Entertainment's other licences (York 7.6%, Morgantown 7.9%, Penn National 5.3% of taxable revenue) host the remaining tier-one skins — trade-press lists put bet365, Fanatics and Penn's own theScore Bet among the 11 live brands alongside BetMGM, Caesars, BetRivers and betPARX, with Mohegan's own online book launched 7 Nov 2025 [brand-to-licence mapping beyond FanDuel/DraftKings unverified this cycle]. BetRivers (Rivers Pittsburgh) took 3.9%, betPARX 1.9%, Harrah's/Caesars 1.8%. Over FY2025/26 Valley Forge generated 41.1% of statewide sports revenue ($272.6m) and the Meadows 28.6% ($189.9m).

PGCB footnotes that gross revenue reflects handle less payouts on wagers settled in the month, so futures distort month-level hold; that said, the Q1 FY26/27 gross hold of 10.4% and taxable hold of 7.5% are consistent with the national shift to parlays. The commercial implication for a challenger is unambiguous: Pennsylvania sports betting is a scale game where the top two brands' promo budgets (together $18.8m in September) exceed the gross revenue of every other licensee combined, the 36% tax plus 0.25% federal excise on handle make low-hold straight-bet books uneconomic, and the policy direction (SGP/microbet bans, VIP and push-notification curbs, advertising hours) targets precisely the product features that drive today's hold expansion. Prediction markets accepting 18-year-olds on sports event contracts outside PGCB's remit are the other volume leak to watch.

Regulatory specifics: sports wagering requires a certificate held by a casino licensee ($10m petition fee; $250k renewal every five years) with online conducted directly or via a licensed sports wagering operator; Category 4 licensees may petition for separate online certificates. Retail books are permitted at casinos and licensed off-track betting sites (Mohegan Lehigh Valley). The 36% tax applies to revenue after promotional credits; there is no handle-based state tax. HB 2879 would add a 0.75% assessment on online sports and casino revenue for problem-gambling programmes.

segments.name: Online casino (iGaming)
segments.headline: $249.3m GGR (+6.8% YoY) on $8.0bn of monthly turnover; three licences (Penn National, Valley Forge/FanDuel, Rivers Philadelphia) hold 83% and the 54% slots tax is softened by deductible promotions.
narrative: Pennsylvania is the largest iGaming market in the United States by regulator-reported GGR and September kept it on a ~$3bn annual run-rate: $249.3m, +6.8% YoY and +1.5% MoM, split $197.4m slots (+9.0%), $49.7m banking tables (−0.6%) and $2.3m poker rake (−1.8%). The deceleration from FY2025/26's +18.4% ($2,933.5m) is visible — Q1 FY26/27 is $744.0m, roughly +8% on the comparable quarter — and reflects a maturing player base (Penn State/DDAP found up to 30% of adults gambled online in 2025) plus supply-side consolidation: Mount Airy ceased iGaming in September 2025, Live! Philadelphia lost 52.8% over the fiscal year and Mohegan was down 64.6% in September.

Turnover data in the PGCB interactive report give an unusually clear view of unit economics. Players wagered $5,115.9m on online slots in September, were paid $4,851.1m and operators booked $197.4m of GGR — a 3.86% hold — which implies about $67.5m (≈25% of pre-deduction win) of promotional credits and other adjustments were netted off before tax; the equivalent implied deduction for Q1 FY26/27 was $213.3m. Banking tables turned over $2,897.9m at a 1.71% hold. Tax is levied on the net figure: 54% on slots (34% state, 13% Commonwealth Financing Authority county grants, 5% local share, 2% local share) and 16% on tables and poker (14% + 2%), producing $114.9m in September (46.1% of iGaming GGR) and $1,337.4m for FY2025/26 (45.6%). The blended effective burden on gross win before promotions is therefore well below the 54% headline, which is why the market has sustained double-digit growth under the highest product tax in the US.

Concentration is extreme. Hollywood Casino at Penn National Race Course's certificate generated $99.0m (39.7%; +12.9% YoY) — this licence hosts multiple third-party skins in addition to Penn's own Hollywood brand [skin roster unverified this cycle] — Valley Forge (FanDuel Casino) $69.8m (28.0%; +5.1%), Rivers Philadelphia (BetRivers) $38.5m (15.4%; +8.6%), Harrah's Philadelphia (Caesars) $13.4m (5.4%; +23.0%). The next tier are Qualified Gaming Entities and smaller skins: Golden Nugget $7.4m (2.9%), Parx/betPARX $5.9m, Bally's $5.4m (+41.7%), Presque Isle $4.7m (+34.8%), Mohegan $2.2m, Live! Philadelphia $2.0m, Wind Creek $1.1m. Over FY2025/26 the shares were 38.6% / 27.7% / 15.8% / 5.5%. Poker remains a niche: $2.3m of rake across Penn National, Valley Forge, Rivers Philadelphia and Harrah's.

Access and cost: interactive gaming certificates are available to the 18 casino licensees and to Qualified Gaming Entities (non-Pennsylvania operators) at $10m for all three verticals or $4m per vertical, with a $4m bond or letter of credit per certificate, $250k renewals every five years, plus a $1m interactive gaming operator (platform) licence ($100k renewal). PGCB counts 22 live iGaming sites; with 11 reporting licensees, that implies two skins per licence on average, and the exits of Mount Airy's and Live!'s partners show skins can be repriced or released. For a B2C entrant the maths only work at tier-one scale or with a differentiated product; for a B2B supplier the 22-site, $3bn market is attractive and the supplier licence is $85k ($75k renewal).

The regulatory overlay is tightening on product and marketing rather than on tax. PGCB's proposed Regulation 125-258 would require deposit, spend, wager and time-limit options at onboarding, hourly session pop-ups, monthly non-promotional RG messaging and marketing opt-outs; the JSG HR60 study and HB 2879 go further with mandatory loss limits (lower for 21–25s), a two-deposit daily cap, affordability checks above $5,000 per 180 days, biometric verification, a VIP/host ban and a credit-card deposit ban. Any of these would compress iGaming yield per active, particularly for the high-value cohorts that the state's own research says generate the bulk of revenue. HB 2801's sweepstakes ban, by contrast, would remove unlicensed competition.

segments.name: Retail casino, VGTs & fantasy
segments.headline: Land-based GGR $256.3m (−3.2% YoY) with tables −18.1%; retail slots flat for three fiscal years — but the October removal of ~70,000 unlicensed skill games is the first genuine demand tailwind in years.
narrative: The 18 land-based casinos won $196.2m on slots (+2.4% YoY; −8.3% MoM on August's seasonally stronger $213.9m) and $60.2m on tables (−18.1%). The slot base is stable: 24,523 machines in service (+192 YoY) at roughly $267 win per unit per day versus $262 a year earlier; FY2025/26 slot GGR of $2,441.0m was +0.02% on FY2024/25 and essentially unchanged since FY2021/22 ($2,410m). Tables have been eroding — $908.9m in FY2025/26 (−2.2%), down from $1,015.7m in FY2021/22 — and September's drop was broad: Wind Creek −23.9%, Parx −29.1%, Rivers Pittsburgh −45.4%, Live! Philadelphia −15.1%, consistent with both low hold and migration of table play online, where iTables GGR ($49.7m) is now 83% of retail tables.

Property dynamics matter for partner selection. On the retail floor Parx is the slot leader ($30.6m; FY $375.2m), followed by Wind Creek Bethlehem ($22.1m; the table leader at $14.1m), Rivers Pittsburgh ($20.1m), Mohegan Pennsylvania ($14.4m) and Mount Airy ($13.2m). The Category 4 mini-casinos — Hollywood York ($6.5m slots), Hollywood Morgantown ($5.1m), Live! Pittsburgh ($7.7m), Parx Shippensburg ($3.3m) and the new Happy Valley Casino in State College ($1.6m slots, $0.4m tables in its sixth month) — are small on the floor but carry sports wagering certificates, which is why Penn's York and Morgantown licences host nationally scaled online sportsbooks. Nemacolin (Category 3) is immaterial at $2.5m.

Taxation of the floor is the heaviest in the country: PGCB-reported slot tax of $99.3m in September is 50.6% of slot GGR (statutory stack: 34% state, Race Horse Development Fund assessment of ~12% by formula, 5% Economic Development & Tourism Fund, 4% local share of which the municipal 2% is replaced for Category 1/2 by a $10m annual licence operation fee), while table tax of $10.5m is 17.4% (14% state + 2% local share; fully automated electronic tables are taxed at a higher rate [unverified]). FY2025/26 slot tax including mandated fees was $1,233.9m and table tax $153.9m.

Video gaming terminals at truck stops remain a sideshow by design: 72 qualified establishments with the maximum five terminals each (74 a year earlier; 75 at FY-end) produced $3.2m (−4.9%) in September and $41.6m in FY2025/26 (+0.6%), taxed at 52% ($1.65m). Marquee by Penn operates 36 sites and took 67% of revenue; J&J Ventures 17 sites, Jango 15, Venture Gaming 4. Fantasy contests were $1.5m (−23.8%; FY $18.0m, −5.8%), 75% DraftKings and 21% FanDuel, taxed at 15%.

The structural swing factor is the skill-game market. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled in June 2026 that the estimated 70,000 'skill' terminals in bars, clubs and convenience stores are slot machines under the Gaming Act; after the legislature let the 13 October deadline lapse, State Police began enforcement on 14 October and the largest supplier, Pace-O-Matic, remotely disabled its machines. Casino and VGT slot play should capture a share of that displaced demand from Q4 2026 — a first material tailwind for a flat retail slot base — but the political consensus (House Speaker McClinton, Senate Republican leaders and Gov. Shapiro all favour taxing and regulating) means a licensed, taxed skill-game or distributed-gaming regime is likely to be legislated in the 2027 session, re-fragmenting the convenience market. Operators should model the Q4 2026–H1 2027 window as a temporary, not permanent, retail uplift.

segments.name: Licensing, tax & operator landscape
segments.headline: Casino-anchored licensing (18 licensees as gatekeepers), GGR-based taxes of 54%/16%/36% unchanged in the FY2026-27 budget, and a record $3.1bn take that lowers near-term rate risk.
narrative: The Pennsylvania Race Horse Development and Gaming Act (4 Pa.C.S., 2004) as expanded by Act 42 of 2017 (HB 271) is the enabling framework; the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board is the single regulator for casinos, iGaming, sports wagering, VGTs and fantasy contests (the Lottery, including iLottery, sits with the Department of Revenue and is outside PGCB's statistics). Land-based licences are capped by category: six Category 1 racetrack casinos, five Category 2 stand-alone, two Category 3 resort and five Category 4 mini-casinos (the Act 42 auction-based satellites, of which Happy Valley opened in April 2026 as the eighteenth casino). Every online product is tethered to those licences: interactive gaming certificates and sports wagering certificates are issued to casino licensees, with Qualified Gaming Entities (out-of-state operators) able to petition for interactive certificates at $4m per vertical when casinos leave them unclaimed — the route Golden Nugget and Bally's used.

Fees are front-loaded and modest relative to revenue: $10m for an interactive gaming certificate covering slots, tables and poker (or $4m each), $10m for a sports wagering certificate, $250k renewals every five years for each, a $4m bond per interactive certificate, $1m for an interactive gaming operator (platform) licence with $100k renewals, $85k/$75k for suppliers, and a $10m annual slot-machine licence operation fee for Category 1/2 casinos that funds local share accounts ($110m in FY2025/26). Principals and key employees are individually licensed ($2,500/$1,500 application fees under the QGE process). Table games required a one-time certificate fee ($2.5m for Category 3 per AGA). Servers and operations must be in Pennsylvania; there is no local-ownership requirement.

Tax is levied on GGR (never on turnover) and is vertical-specific. Online slots carry 54% (34% state gaming fund, 13% CFA county grants, 5% and 2% local share assessments); online tables and poker 16% (14% + 2%); sports wagering 36% (34% + 2%) of revenue after promotional credits, on top of the 0.25% federal excise on handle; retail slots roughly 55% statutory (34% state, ~12% Race Horse Development Fund, 5% EDTF, 4% local) with PGCB's September figures showing 50.6% effective; retail tables 16% (17.4% effective); VGTs 52%; fantasy 15% of adjusted revenue. Promotional credits are deductible for sports and iGaming. September 2026 produced $242.6m of tax and local share (43.7% of GGR); FY2025/26 produced $3,098.2m (44.2%) — slots $1,233.9m, iGaming $1,337.4m, sports $238.7m, tables $153.9m, VGT $21.6m, DFS $2.7m. Proceeds fund school property-tax relief, local share grants, horse racing and the General Fund.

The operator landscape is concentrated and casino-controlled. By September total revenue: Penn Entertainment's six properties (Penn National $113.6m, Meadows $27.5m, York $10.6m, Morgantown $8.9m, plus Marquee VGTs) ≈ 29% of the state; Boyd's Valley Forge $96.6m (17.4%) via FanDuel; Rush Street's Rivers Philadelphia and Pittsburgh $81.2m; Greenwood's Parx and Shippensburg $53.6m; Wind Creek $37.5m; Caesars' Harrah's $24.4m; Cordish's Live! Philadelphia and Pittsburgh $30.3m; Mohegan $18.8m; Mount Airy $15.8m; Churchill Downs' Presque Isle $14.2m; Bally's $5.4m (QGE); Golden Nugget $7.4m (QGE). FY2025/26 iGaming shares: Penn National 38.6%, Valley Forge 27.7%, Rivers Philadelphia 15.8%; sports: Valley Forge 41.1%, Meadows 28.6%. Eleven online sportsbook brands and 22 iGaming sites operate across these licences.

Direction of travel on the fiscal side is stable: the $50.8bn FY2026-27 budget signed in July 2026 contained no gaming tax changes, and a record take reduces appetite for rate increases. Two legislative vehicles nonetheless carry tax and fee language — HB 2801 (2027 session) is drafted as a Gaming Act rewrite 'revising licensing fees, taxes and revenue distributions' alongside its sweepstakes ban, and any skill-game legalisation will set a new terminal tax rate (Shapiro has proposed taxing the devices in three of four budgets; the rate has been the sticking point). HB 2879 would add a 0.75% RG assessment on online revenue. For an entrant, the licensing risk is less about fees than about shelf space: access depends on an incumbent casino partner or a QGE certificate, and skins have been released (Mount Airy, Live!) rather than added.

segments.name: Responsible gambling, payments & regulatory direction
segments.headline: The 2027 agenda is written: PGCB Regulation 125-258, HB 2879's mandatory limits/credit-card and VIP bans, a sweepstakes ban (HB 2801), unresolved prediction-market jurisdiction and skill-game re-legalisation.
narrative: Pennsylvania's responsible-gambling framework is moving from opt-in tools to prescriptive controls, driven by state-funded evidence. The Penn State/DDAP 2025 Interactive Gaming Assessment (published January 2026, funded from Act 42 iGaming levies) found that up to 30% of adults gambled online in 2025 versus 20% in 2024 and ~11% in 2021-22, that 2.5–6.4% of Pennsylvanians may be problem gamblers, that dual-mode (online and offline) players carry the highest risk and that more than 10% of adults used unregulated sites. The Joint State Government Commission's HR60 staff study (14 July 2026) converted that into recommendations: a player-level data mandate first, then a uniform credit-card deposit ban for interactive accounts (slot play is already card-free under 58 Pa. Code), mandatory rather than optional loss, session and deposit-count limits, a ban on promotions to logged-off customers, and curtailment of VIP programmes; in-game betting restrictions received only passing mention.

PGCB's own response is proposed Regulation #125-258 (Pennsylvania Bulletin, 11 July 2026; comments closed 10 August; IRRC review in progress). It would require interactive and sports operators to offer daily, weekly and monthly deposit, spend, wager and time limits at account opening, applicable separately or jointly to iGaming and sports; hourly pop-ups showing time and amount wagered that the player must dismiss; monthly messages on limits, tools and help resources free of advertising; a direct-marketing opt-out; account suspension of up to a year; monthly licensee reporting on self-limiting and self-exclusion; and a formal advertising rule for audiences that are majority under-age. Greenwood (Parx) filed comments; the National Council on Problem Gambling (29 July) is pressing for limits to be default-on. Final adoption in 2027 is the base case.

The legislature is going further. HB 2879, the Pennsylvania Online Consumer Protection Act (introduced 21 October 2026 by Reps. Tarik Khan (D) and Jamie Flick (R), referred to House Gaming Oversight), would ban microbets and same-game parlays, VIP/host and play-more-earn-more programmes, credit-card funding and automatic wagering; mandate daily and monthly loss limits (lower for 21–25-year-olds), cap deposits at two per day, require affordability checks before more than $5,000 of deposits in 180 days, default sessions to two hours per day with a 72-hour wait to raise limits, require biometric verification at login and for wagers above $500, restrict advertising hours and ban ads using athletes, celebrities or influencers appealing to minors, regulate AI-driven promotions, and levy 0.75% of online casino and sports revenue to fund DDAP programmes. With two House session days left before 30 November and no carry-over, it will not pass in 2025-26; its bipartisan sponsorship and the new Problem Gambling Caucus make it the reference text for 2027. Advertising is otherwise governed by PGCB regulations and self-regulation; there is no statutory watershed today.

Payments: PGCB publishes no payment-mix statistics (n/a). Interactive accounts may be funded by credit card, debit, ACH/online banking, e-wallets and cage or prepaid options; cash withdrawals are available at partner casino cages. The credit-card ban has three independent sponsors (JSG, HB 2879, and the HR60 advisory committee consensus) and should be treated as probable within 12–18 months, with knock-on effects on first-deposit conversion and on the share of deposits routed through debit/ACH. Mandatory affordability checks above $5,000 per 180 days would, if enacted as drafted, formalise source-of-funds processes at a lower threshold than most US states.

Three other fronts shape competitive intensity. First, unlicensed online supply: HB 2801 (pre-filed late September for the 5 January 2027 session; Rep. Russ Diamond, co-chair of House Gaming Oversight, with four co-sponsors) would outlaw dual-currency sweepstakes casinos with fines up to $500,000 and give PGCB and the Attorney General investigative powers — net positive for licensees. Second, prediction markets: Kalshi and Polymarket accept Pennsylvanians aged 18+ under CFTC designation; PGCB wrote to the CFTC on 30 April 2026 that sports event contracts 'is sports wagering' and Executive Director Kevin O'Toole warned legislators of the integrity risk, but PGCB has not issued a cease-and-desist (the CFTC has backed Kalshi against New York and Michigan orders), and HB 2711 (22 July 2026) would instead license such markets under the Attorney General at $1m with a 21+ floor. Third, skill games: with ~70,000 terminals ordered dark from 14 October 2026 and seizures under way, the 2027 session will almost certainly revisit a regulated, taxed regime — the rate (Shapiro has pushed for taxation in three of four budgets; the industry has argued for far lower rates) is the unresolved variable. The November 2026 gubernatorial election (Shapiro vs Garrity) determines who signs it.

highlights.text: Scale and penetration: $7.0bn FY2025/26 GGR (+9.6%), online above 50% of revenue, iGaming $2.93bn (+18.4%) and still +6.8% in September — the deepest regulated online casino pool in the US for any supplier or skin partner.

Skill-game removal: ~70,000 unlicensed terminals ordered dark from 14 Oct 2026 after the Supreme Court ruling — a first genuine demand tailwind for licensed slots (24,523 units, flat for three years), VGTs and iGaming through at least H1 2027.

Sports betting hold expansion: taxable hold 7.85% in FY2025/26 vs 5.59%, September gross hold 9.2% — revenue +36% FY and +50% YoY in September on declining handle, so the revenue pool grows without volume.

Promotional deductibility: $28.8m of sports credits and an implied ~$67.5m of iSlots deductions netted off before tax in September — the 54%/36% headline rates bite on a materially smaller base than gross win.

Sweepstakes ban (HB 2801) pre-filed for the January 2027 session with $500k fines and PGCB/AG enforcement — would remove the main unlicensed online casino competitor; >10% of adults currently use unregulated sites.

Qualified Gaming Entity route: non-casino brands can hold iGaming certificates at $4m per vertical (Golden Nugget, Bally's precedent) and released skins (Mount Airy, Live!) create shelf space; supplier licence is only $85k.
Fiscal stability: FY2026-27 budget left 54%/16%/36% untouched and a record $3.1bn take lowers the political appetite for rate increases in 2027.

lowlights.text: Heaviest tax stack in US iGaming: 54% on online slots, 46% blended effective on iGaming GGR, 36% on sports plus 0.25% federal excise, ~55% statutory on retail slots — margins only work at tier-one scale.

Concentration: top three iGaming licences hold 83.1%; FanDuel and DraftKings hold 68.6% of online sports revenue and spent $18.8m on promos in September — more than every other licensee's gross revenue combined. Presque Isle's new skin needed promo equal to 86% of gross to reach 5% of handle.

Consumer-protection pipeline: HB 2879 (SGP/microbet ban, VIP ban, credit-card ban, mandatory loss limits, affordability checks >$5k/180d, biometrics, 0.75% RG levy) plus PGCB Regulation 125-258 and the JSG HR60 recommendations — bipartisan, evidence-backed and aimed at the exact drivers of current yield.

Volume leakage: sports handle −6.1% YoY in September and −3.1% over FY2025/26 while prediction markets (Kalshi, Polymarket) take sports event contracts from 18-year-olds outside PGCB's tax and RG regime; PGCB has no enforcement tool yet.

Retail erosion: retail tables −18.1% YoY in September and −2.2% FY; retail casino GGR −3.2%; land-based slots have been flat since FY2021/22 — the skill-game uplift is likely temporary once a taxed regime is legislated in 2027.

Political and fiscal re-opening risk: HB 2801 is drafted as a Gaming Act rewrite of fees, taxes and distributions; any skill-game legalisation will set a new terminal tax and could extend distributed gaming; the November 2026 gubernatorial election decides who signs.
Small verticals shrinking: fantasy −23.8% YoY ($1.5m), VGTs −4.9% with sites down 74→72, poker −1.8% — no diversification cushion outside iGaming slots and sports.

forecast.intro: The bridge from FY2025/26's record $7,006m to FY2026/27 is driven by online casino and policy, not by land-based volume. Q1 FY26/27 (Jul–Sep) is tracking iGaming at $744.0m (~+8%) and sports taxable revenue at $135.9m on a 7.5% hold, while retail casino is running −3% to −4%. Three moving parts dominate the next 12–18 months: (1) iGaming growth settling into high single digits as penetration plateaus and skins consolidate; (2) a one-off retail slot/VGT uplift from the removal of ~70,000 skill games from 14 Oct 2026 that reverses if Harrisburg legalises a taxed regime in 2027; and (3) regulatory drag on yield from PGCB Regulation 125-258 and whichever parts of HB 2879 (credit-card ban, mandatory limits, VIP/SGP curbs, 0.75% levy) survive the 2027 session. Tax rates themselves are the least likely variable to move.

forecast.view: Our independent view (all figures estimates): **FY2026/27 total gaming revenue of $7.3–7.5bn (+4–7%)**, with iGaming $3.15–3.26bn, sports taxable revenue $630–720m on handle of $8.0–8.4bn (hold 7.5–8.5%), retail slots $2.46–2.54bn and tables $870–890m; **tax and fees $3.2–3.3bn**, effective ~44% of GGR. On rules: **PGCB Regulation 125-258 is finalised in H1 2027 with opt-in (not default) limits**, hourly pop-ups and monthly RG messaging; **a credit-card deposit ban for interactive accounts is the most probable statutory change in 2027** (three independent sponsors), followed by advertising restrictions and some form of mandatory limit or affordability check; a full SGP/microbet ban is less likely to survive given it would cut the state's fastest-growing tax line, but a 0.75% RG levy is a plausible compromise. **Skill-game legalisation with a terminal tax is more likely than not in 2027** — the fight is the rate — which caps the retail uplift to roughly two to three quarters. **A sweepstakes ban (HB 2801) is likely** in some form; prediction markets remain unresolved pending federal litigation, and PGCB is more likely to seek legislative authority than to issue cease-and-desists. Tax rates on licensed products stay at 54%/16%/36%. For B2Tech the implication is to **enter as a platform/content supplier or via a QGE/skin partnership priced for 46% blended iGaming tax and a 2027 promo/VIP squeeze**, and to treat Pennsylvania sports betting as a FanDuel/DraftKings market where third-brand economics require sub-30% promo-to-gross discipline.
watch: PGCB Regulation #125-258: IRRC disposition and final-form publication (expected H1 2027) — whether limits are opt-in or default-on, and the under-age-audience advertising rule.
HB 2879 successor bill in the 2027-28 session (opens 5 Jan 2027): credit-card ban, SGP/microbet language, VIP ban, 0.75% RG levy, affordability threshold; House Gaming Oversight hearing schedule.

Skill-game legislation and tax rate after the Supreme Court ruling; State Police enforcement progress (6 operator agreements) and any renewed stay; Q4 2026 retail slot and VGT revenue as the displacement signal.
HB 2801 sweepstakes ban and its embedded Gaming Act fee/tax/distribution rewrite — the one vehicle that could reopen rates.
Prediction markets: PGCB vs CFTC posture, HB 2711 progress, and any Pennsylvania cease-and-desist or litigation; monthly online handle trend (−6.1% in September).
Monthly PGCB releases (~20th of each month): iGaming YoY growth staying above ~6%; sports taxable hold vs the 7.5–8.5% band; promo credits as % of handle (3.6% in September).
Skin movements: Penn National's third-party iGaming roster, Presque Isle's new online brand economics, further exits after Mount Airy, and the Mohegan online sportsbook ramp.
November 2026 gubernatorial election (Shapiro vs Garrity) and FY2027-28 budget address (Feb 2027) for any gaming revenue proposals.

report.confidenceNote: Data confidence HIGH for all GGR, handle, promo-credit and tax figures: taken from PGCB's 19 Oct 2026 release, the FY2025/26 release (17 Jul 2026), the 2025-26 Annual Report release (30 Sep 2026) and the FY26/27 Monthly Sports Wagering and Interactive Gaming reports; component taxes reconcile to the reported $242,630,497 and tax-line percentages confirm the 54%/16%/36%/52%/15% rates. MEDIUM for: (i) the implied iSlots deduction (derived as wagers − payouts − GGR, not a reported line); (ii) retail-slot statutory sub-rates (Race Horse Development Fund share varies by formula; PGCB effective 50.6%); (iii) brand-to-licence mapping — only FanDuel→Valley Forge and DraftKings→Meadows corroborated by two sources, other skin assignments and the Presque Isle brand are [unverified]; (iv) the ~70,000 skill-game estimate (Spotlight PA/court coverage) and the electronic-table tax differential [unverified]. Not obtained this cycle: PA Lottery/iLottery figures, PGCB payment-mix data, PGCB fines and self-exclusion counts for 2026 (all n/a). Reporting currency USD — no FX conversion required.
